en: Dense night full of darkness — no direction, none at all —
Alone on the deep-dark road, traveler, where do you go?
You know no danger or sorrow, you heed no obstacle,
you are crossing the darkness — whose call do you hear?
A lamp burns in your heart; no force of wind will quench it —
in great joy, unceasing, what song is this you sing?
Fearlessness before you, a fearless cry behind —
within and without, toward whose face do you gaze?
Alas, alas, alas, exile,
alas, homeless wanderer.
At the call of blind fate
where do you drift toward an unknown shoreless deep?
Do you hear, in the far sky, on some wind,
the flute of ruin —
oh, the merciless hunter weaves the noose of death.
Beneath colored clouds, in hidden tears,
in God's terrible thunderbolt of mockery,
lies stored a silent roar of laughter.
Who will undo the bonds of the beautiful from the cruel one's hand?
Who will wipe the tears of the helpless from the eyes of the oppressed?
Behold the earth aggrieved by the weeping of the afflicted,
riddled with poisoned arrows by the assault of injustice —
from the tyranny of the mighty
who will save the weak?
Whose mercy will call the humiliated to its breast?
In the sky your freedom waits as ever,
let not your two wings lie idle.
O bird, beneath the dense forest
the nest keeps you beguiled by trickery,
the night tells you falsely
that its grip will never loosen.
Do you not know for what hope
you rise singing, singing, in the daze of sleep?
Do you not know, in the dark of dawn,
the hope of light sounds in a deep tone,
the hope of light will not stay hidden —
bursting the bonds of the shut bud.
Where do you wander in quest of the ultimate end?
As the endless, he is here in this very world.
His word stretches out two arms in a child's guise,
calls in half-formed speech, coming to your breast,
his touch has fallen on that flower garden.
Where do you wander in quest of your own kin —
as a stranger he shows himself moment by moment.
His dwelling is at the outer door of every house,
his light is along the edge of every road,
his form, in hidden form, is in person after person.
Look and see the play of colors on the stream of delight.
Do not wish, do not wish to draw it near.
What you wish to keep, wish to bind,
melts into the dark, melts again and again —
what sounded on the vina-strings of the soul
is only song, only word.
Its touch is not to be had, nor any measure —
the nectar the gods drink in their court.
In the river's current, in grove after grove of flowers,
in a sweetness-laden smile, in an eye's corner,
drink that drop of nectar in your own heart —
take it, know it, in its free form.
The beggar who stays empty-handed at day's end
shows himself in the dead of night in the guise of dream.
He whom in the light I see dull-faced and silent —
when dark falls, what radiance is this in his eyes —
who sways a garland of welcome in his hair?
The faint string neglected on the day's vina
rings out resounding in the night.
In the vast song of sleepless darkness
the whole sky swells deep-toned with what summons —
who keeps gazing unblinking in the starlight?
What madman goes, goes along your road, goes on through that lonely night —
do not call him, do not call him into your courtyard.
Word of a far-off land, he says 'I go, I go' — alas, who understands —
what tune he plays on his one-stringed lute.
Tomorrow morning he will not stay, will not stay,
why spread a seat in vain?
At the great festival of breaking bonds
he must sing his song
in praise of the new light.
Exile, come away home
on the favoring breeze.
Look, how many times the ferry has crossed,
the boatmen's chorus has risen to the sky.
In sky upon sky the preparations,
in wind upon wind the invitation.
Your heart gave no answer, so you are homeless,
banished without and within.
What dwelt in the darkness of the soul
has come to the shore of the world's light.
Bursting the bonds of dream it came running out,
two astonished eyes beheld it.
I had strung a garland with streams of tears,
with that enchanted chain I had bound it.
The one I worshipped in silent pain, alas —
all the universe sings praise of him.
The weeping with which my heart weeps — with that weeping he too wept.
The bond with which he binds me — with that bond he was bound.
I sought him road after road, I worshipped him in my heart,
and hidden within that worship he wooed me too.
He had come to steal my heart, crossing the great ocean.
He returned no more to his boat; he lost himself.
His own sweetness plays its trick upon himself,
will he capture or be captured — with what thought did he lay the snare?
We are the band of Lakshmi's outcasts — water on the lotus leaf of the world,
forever trembling and tottering,
our coming and going is empty wind, with no result at all.
We know no ways or means, we know no manner or measure,
we heed no rule or restraint, oh —
by our own defiance, on the whim of the mind, we have torn our chains.
Lakshmi, let your mounts swell up with wealth and sons,
let them roll in your foot-dust, oh —
we, with quilt and satchel on our shoulders, will roam the earth.
At your harbor's moored quay, on barges loaded with gold,
many jewels in many markets, oh —
we are only broken boats with torn anchors, adrift.
Now let us search and see if a shore is found in the shoreless,
if there is an island in the sea of being.
If no joy comes our way, we will dive and see where the abyss lies.
Gathering all day long, we will hold a fair of the luckless,
we will sing songs, we will play games, oh —
and if no song comes to our throats, we will raise a clamor.
Oh, you are all good —
whatever fate has dealt to each, that is good for us —
light the evening lamp in this dark house of ours.
Some blaze bright, some are dim and brimming with tears,
some scorch a little, some are a soothing light.
A new bride in new love is honey through and through,
the old is sweet-and-sour, just a little sharp.
When words dismiss you, the eyes come clasp your feet,
pour out anger and affection in equal shares.
We are thirst, you are nectar — you are contentment, we are hunger —
in speaking of you the poet's words ran out.
Whatever image rises before my eyes, I love them all —
some divinely fair, some divinely dark.
Good folk we are not, no, good folk we are not —
that is our one virtue, that is our one virtue.
Slander spreads from land to land, danger strikes at every step —
we do not speak the words of scripture, we speak them upside down.
We were born under an evil conjunction, all misbegotten.
Jupiter took his leave; Saturn's gaze remained.
We launch the boat at an ill-omened hour; brother, we keep no hope of gain —
we have no course left but to drift on.
Whom should we fear?
What can old, old thieves and robbers do to us?
Our road is straight, no alleys — no satchel, no purse —
let them snatch whatever else they will; no one will snatch our madness.
We want no comfort, we want no rest,
we want no reward, we want no fame —
we dance the same in rising and falling,
we play the same in winning and losing.
Our hair will not turn grey, oh — our hair will not turn grey.
Our flowers will not fall, oh — our flowers will not fall.
We will run up against no end; the road runs out in no land,
our errors will not cease, oh — our errors will not cease.
Eyes closed, we will not meditate, will not meditate.
In our own mind's corner we will not seek wisdom, will not seek wisdom.
We drift on from current to current, from the peak toward the sea,
we will find no shore, oh — we will find no shore.
I fall at your feet — listen, brother singer,
keep a little distance from our neighborhood as you pass.
Here the sa re ga ma are forever pulling each other's hair,
sharps and flats have sunk out of sight somewhere.
Here there is a beat-breaking player —
he will start a brawl.
In chautal and dhamar
who strikes a blow where —
tere-kete, slash-and-smite, dha-dha-dhaiye.
O brother Kanai, to whom shall I tell my unbearable sorrow?
I have passed three or four degrees; I am no utter fool.
A trifling sa-re-ga-ma makes me sweat and drip.
Whatever my brains may be, my two ears are not fine —
this is my great sorrow, Kanai,
this is my great sorrow.
To sing a song to my sweetheart I must call in Satish,
my poor heart spins to death on a gramophone disc.
My voice has strength, so I dare not sing even in hiding —
my beloved herself says, 'Your voice is terribly harsh' —
this is my great sorrow, Kanai,
this is my great sorrow.
The tone-deaf goddess who roams the thorn-woods —
we serve her feet, to her we sing our worship,
we few, dwellers in the land of bad voices.
Our gathering is in the town of renouncers, far from raga and ragini,
by the practice of past lives we have brought this learning with us, oh —
reveling at the bottom of the tuneless abyss.
Seventeen generations have gone; the broken tanpura
remains gathering rust, forlorn and out of tune.
Two stringless sitars, the tabla cracked and full of holes,
with these we perform our rites to the crusher of tunes —
we are imagination.
We are the band of no-song-singers, we of the never-trained voice.
At our raga Bhairo the morning sun darkens its face in rage.
Under the blows of this clashing-voice cooperative of ours
the neighborhood dogs, O brother, burst out whimpering in fear, all in one voice —
we only die of fear of elder brother Dhurjati.
If we strike up Megh Mallar, drought follows,
and Saturn's gaze falls across the umbrella-seller's shop.
The moment we hit half a note of Basanta Bahar
the south wind's temper turns; that instant, alas,
on that breeze the fever of parting flees from Sri Radha.
The moment we sit down to sing Behag on a moonless night
the cuckoos fall into their death throes.
On the bright Kojagari night we strike up Jayjayanti,
and at once, alas, alas,
the pain of Rahu's seizing grips the full moon.
We have nothing, nothing at all; we sing at home and abroad —
taire naire naire na. Na na na.
However the days go by, we sing on in joy — alas, alas —
taire naire naire na. Na na na.
Those who build solid house-foundations on golden quicksand —
before them we go singing our song — taire naire naire na.
Na na na.
When now and then the cutpurses dart glances at our purse-knots,
then, showing our empty bags, we sing — taire naire naire na. Na na na.
When old crone Death comes to the door, we snap our fingers in her face,
then, brother, we strike up the song with a flourish — taire naire naire na. Na na na.
See, King Spring has come today, his dress outside is brilliant,
and oh, within him a renouncer sings — taire naire naire na. Na na na.
He, having ended the festive day, having shed all, having withered all,
beats time with two empty hands and sings — taire naire naire na.
Na na na.
Now, finding Death's door open, all the boys and girls have run out.
Haribol, Hari bol, haribol.
A mighty game across the kingdom, careless of life and death —
O brother, when all give their lives together, what joy is greater than that death?
Haribol, Hari bol, haribol.
The dhol has sounded, the dhak has sounded, the call has gone from house to house,
now let work and business go to the ashes — come running, all you busy folk.
Haribol, Hari bol, haribol.
King and subject will gather; there will be no more small and great —
in one same current all will float in joy down the river Vaitarani.
Haribol, Hari bol, haribol.
Alas, alas, alas — the day slips away.
Restless tea-craving flock of chataks — come, come, come along!
Bubbling and boiling, the water in the kettle gurgles and sings.
From the skies of China, on the stream of the east wind, the dark clouds heavy with brew have come.
On this monsoon day the brew pours streaming down — drink, oh drink, all you company!
Come, keeper of books, master of suffix and case — savior, you are the helmsman.
Come, champion of mathematics, lord of poetry, treasurer of geography.
Come, you bowed beneath the world's burden, weary of pacing the desert of dry routine.
Come, you terrified of account-books, plagued by untallied funds, the corners of your eyes brimming with tears.
Come, walker of song's avenues, tanpura in hand, sunk deep in tan and tal.
Come, painter — quick now, drop your brush and canvas — you engrossed in line and color.
Come, you adorned with constitutional rules, untiring in debate.
Come, fugitive from committees, slayer of statutes — come, bewildered and tottering one!
O goddess Fortune, grandmother, my hopes are done —
now give the command, and your servant will take his leave.
This bridal lamp of life burns down, it seems; the light will go out —
no sight of the bride, only mockery in plenty.
Now the flute has fallen silent, the heaps of flowers have withered,
and your roaring laughter has risen, shaking the sky.
Those who thronged around me have gone back each to their homes,
and you remain, old dame, your veil drawn over your face.
His airs make one laugh — alas, alas!
Amid the preparations for death, on what business does he sit —
this venerable, ancient expatriate — alas, alas!
Now, on the day of going home, let him come to know himself,
all together dress him up as an ascetic of youthful form — alas, alas!
Now plunge him into the dire tangle of mistaken accounts.
Snatch away his bags and platters, come bearing baskets of flowers,
and set the madman of his secret heart out in the open today — alas, alas!
